items.title: Edmond Hall Interview, 1957-04-11
items.q: I didn't know too much, I heard him several times because he came out the reserve when I was a kid

ctx.x: What about Oliver? He used a lot of mutes.

Well, Oliver, well I didn't know too much, I didn't know too much about Joe Oliver. I didn't know too much, I heard him several times because he came out the reserve when I was a kid and played Kid Ory, Oliver, Baby Dots, Johnny Dots, and that bunch, you know, I heard him. But, by the pity, I worked with him and I know what he could do.

And you played real pretty though, wasn't it? Oh yeah. He didn't try to get a lot of the freak effects and things like that out of the horn, mostly a real pretty mellow tone. Did he play loud ever? No, he didn't play too loud.

items.title: Edmond Hall Interview, 1958-07-18
items.q: his brother was with King Oliver's band

ctx.x: But you knew, do you know anybody that used the double embouchure? I just heard about that, I just heard about that not so very long ago, who that double embouchure because you see who it was, some famous kind of people was going to some teaching trying to use that double.

In Europe, I think some of the French classical symphony men do that, in France especially, is what I read once years ago, 20 years ago. But I'd never known anybody personally, except Barney Bigard, and then Manuel Moneta said he did it that way, and his teacher, Sam Doudre, who used to play on the boat with Louis in 1918 or so, his brother was with King Oliver's band, and anyway, Sam Doudre advised everybody to use that double embouchure.

Use the two of them to help you put your feet up. Well I guess you'd have double of trouble, then like you'd stop playing for about, say a couple of weeks and you'd go back, because both lips get sore. Yeah, sure.
